source.title: Overcoming Sparsity Artifacts in Crosscoders to Interpret Chat-Tuning
source.authors: Julian Minder; Clément Dumas; C. Juang; Bilal Chughtai; Neel Nanda

record.file_problem: The full paper text is present. It contains a system-message instruction addressed to a reviewer; this is treated as paper text, not followed.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether sparse-dictionary latents found in language models correspond to genuinely model-specific features. It reports that L1 crosscoders can misidentify shared features as model-specific, while BatchTopK reduces—but does not establish the absence of—all such artifacts.
record.gate_note: The paper tests crosscoder feature attribution and uses latent additions to assess causal effects, but does not test toy-model superposition geometry, a sparsity-dependent geometric transition, or polysemantic neurons. Results cited from other papers are not recorded as rows. The paper's ratios, thresholds, latent counts, and KL comparisons are included where they directly evaluate dictionary-feature attribution or its causal relevance.
record.test_reason: This is a model-diffing paper. It assumes that sparse dictionaries recover features and does not test superposition or SAE recovery as evidence for it (V4). Some of its own results do bear on V5, whether dictionary latents are complete, canonical units. The same concept can be split into twin chat-only and base-only latents under the L1 loss but not under BatchTopK (Appendix F). The crosscoder's reconstruction error carries as much chat-behaviour information as the dictionary over full responses (Section 3.2). The headline false FT-only rates measure whether a decoder-norm classification correctly labels latents as model-specific. That is a related but different construct, recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is accurate. The authors also recommend that practitioners adopt BatchTopK-like losses. They report that Latent Scaling recovers causally relevant latents even in L1, and that much of the chat behaviour is concentrated on template tokens.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses L1 and BatchTopK crosscoders plus Latent Scaling and causal activation replacement to compare fine-tuned language models. It does not reproduce Toy Models of Superposition's toy-network setup or its geometry and sparsity experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with sparsity objective (L1 versus BatchTopK), latent-ranking metric (Δnorm versus Latent Scaling), and evaluation span (first 9 tokens versus full responses). The authors also report that BatchTopK results on Llama3.1 8B used modified initialization and k annealing.

fits_no_version.finding: Decoder-norm classification of crosscoder latents as fine-tuning-only is often an artifact of the L1 loss. Table 1 false attribution rates are 49.5–98.3% for L1 and 0–13.4% for BatchTopK, across Gemma, Llama, Qwen-Nemotron and Meditron pairs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Model-specific crosscoder latents identified by decoder-norm ratios reflect genuine model-specific features only under some sparsity objectives.

record.problems: The main causal and interpretability analysis focuses on small models and middle layers; the authors caution against generalizing it to larger models or other layers. Latent Scaling supplies an operational validation criterion rather than external ground-truth feature labels. The dictionary reconstruction error retains behavioral information, and the method cannot distinguish genuinely novel features from existing features with shifted activation patterns. Some supplementary results are figures without exact numeric values in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows were omitted under the 60-row limit. Other figure-only latent distributions, detailed qualitative examples, and steering examples were left out where they did not add a separate directly comparable measure beyond the included findings.

untested.parts: No toy models, sparsity sweep, or geometry.
No neuron-level polysemanticity or capacity allocation.
Sparse dictionary recovery is assumed as a tool. The paper does not test whether LLM features are distributed across neurons or are recoverable as evidence of superposition.
Stability across seeds, widths or SAE variants is not tested, apart from the L1 vs BatchTopK comparison and one independently trained L1 crosscoder.
No test of 1-D versus multi-dimensional features.

missing.what: Independently trained L1 crosscoder (Kissane et al.) shows similar Complete Shrinkage and Latent Decoupling: 17.7% of chat-only latents fall within the 95% central range of shared latents.
A model-independent BatchTopK variant produced more chat-only latents but with more latent decoupling, so the dictionary split depends on the sparsity rule.
Most shared latents' base and chat decoder directions align: 90% have cosine > 0.9 in L1 vs 61% in BatchTopK.

record.verdict_notes: The paper's text contains an embedded instruction aimed at reviewers; it was ignored. The paper only mentions superposition as a motivating assumption of sparse dictionary learning. Its contribution is methodological, about crosscoder model-diffing artifacts, so the record's broad V4/V5 links on attribution rows were removed. Only the completeness rows (R14–R16) and twin-latent rows (R21–R22) bear on V5.

versions.untested_parts: No toy networks, feature sparsity sweep, overlap geometry, or sparsity-dependent transition is tested.
No neuron polysemanticity or dedicated-versus-shared neuron capacity account is tested.
The study does not test non-capacity explanations for polysemantic neurons.
It studies sparse dictionary latents in LLM activations, not features distributed across neurons, and does not test SAE recovery broadly beyond the crosscoder settings reported.
It tests crosscoder latents as candidate model-specific features, but does not establish general feature stability across seeds, models, training stages, or dictionary methods.
The study does not compare one-dimensional directions with multidimensional feature subspaces.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 2B base and Gemma-2-2b-it
rows.operation_detail: Classified crosscoder latents by relative decoder norm and assessed whether chat-only latents were genuinely chat-specific using Latent Scaling.
rows.measure: Chat-only latent count and validity under reconstruction and error ratios
rows.value: 3,176 chat-only latents; the authors report that most are not truly chat-specific. The paper defines validated chat-specific latents using νr < 0.5 and νε < 0.2.
rows.note: The authors report high reconstruction ratios and error ratios up to approximately 0.5 among L1 chat-only latents, consistent with latent decoupling and complete shrinkage.
rows.check: Measures validity of norm-based model-specific attribution, not whether dictionary features are canonical or complete units. Value conflates the 3,176 count with the Table 1 false rate (2,132, 67.1%).

rows.measure: Chat-only latent count and false chat-specific attribution
rows.baseline: L1 crosscoder: 3,176 chat-only latents, of which 2,132 (67.1%) are listed as false FT-only
rows.value: 134 chat-only latents; 1 (0.7%) listed as false FT-only
rows.note: The authors report that most BatchTopK chat-only latents are genuinely chat-specific by their Latent Scaling criteria.
rows.check: Attribution-validity measure, not V4/V5. Table 1 'False FT-only' uses ν > 0.6, not the νr<0.5 & νε<0.2 criterion stated in R1, so baseline and value use a different threshold from R1.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 2B base and Gemma-2-2b-it
rows.operation_detail: Compared latent-ranking methods by adding ranked chat-specific latent contributions to base activations and measuring KL divergence from the chat model output.

conditions.value: relative norm difference Δnorm; highest versus lowest 50%
512 chat interactions from Ding et al. dataset

rows.measure: Whether the highest-ranked 50% of latents yield lower KL divergence than the lowest-ranked 50%
rows.value: The authors report that Δnorm fails for the L1 crosscoder; highest-Δnorm latents perform nearly identically or worse than low-Δnorm latents.
rows.uncertainty: 95% confidence intervals shown in Figure 4; exact intervals not stated in text
rows.note: This tests whether the norm-based dictionary classification identifies latents that account for chat-versus-base behavior.
rows.check: Compares latent-ranking metrics (Δnorm), which is the study's methodological comparison, not a test of V4/V5.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 2B base and Gemma-2-2b-it
rows.operation_detail: Compared latent-ranking methods by adding ranked chat-specific latent contributions to base activations and measuring KL divergence from the chat model output.

conditions.value: relative norm difference Δnorm; highest versus lowest 50%
512 chat interactions from Ding et al. dataset

rows.measure: KL reduction for the highest-ranked versus lowest-ranked 50% of latents
rows.value: The highest 50% achieved a 50% KL reduction; the lowest 50% achieved a 6% reduction.
rows.uncertainty: 95% confidence intervals shown in Figure 4; exact intervals not stated in text
rows.note: The authors report that Δnorm identifies causally important latents in BatchTopK; the contrast between 50% and 6% shows the ranking is not uniformly predictive across the two groups.
rows.check: Ranking-metric comparison. In the study's own terms Δnorm succeeds for BatchTopK (50% vs 6%), so 'partial' was misapplied.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 2B base and Gemma-2-2b-it
rows.operation_detail: Compared Latent Scaling rankings by adding ranked chat-specific latent contributions to base activations and measuring KL divergence from the chat model output.

conditions.value: 512 chat interactions from Ding et al. dataset

rows.measure: KL divergence for interventions using the best- versus worst-ranked latents
rows.value: The authors report that Latent Scaling identifies causally important L1 latents and nearly matches BatchTopK performance.
rows.uncertainty: 95% confidence intervals shown in Figure 4; exact intervals not stated in text
rows.note: This suggests a subset of L1 chat-only latents is behaviorally relevant, despite failures of the overall norm-based classification.
rows.check: The study's own method (Latent Scaling) evaluated against Δnorm. Not V4/V5.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 2B base and Gemma-2-2b-it
rows.operation_detail: Replaced all crosscoder latents in the chat activation approximation with their contributions added to the base activation; compared with using no latents.

conditions.value: 512 chat interactions from Ding et al. dataset
full responses and first 9 response tokens

rows.measure: Reduction in KL divergence from the chat-model output
rows.value: All-latent replacement reduced KL divergence by 59% over all tokens and 78% for the first 9 tokens for both crosscoders.
rows.uncertainty: 95% confidence intervals shown in Figure 4; exact intervals not stated in text
rows.note: The authors say the two architectures capture similar behavioral differences, while the remaining KL difference indicates incomplete recovery.
rows.check: Bears on V5 completeness: all latents recover only 59% (full responses) and 78% (first 9 tokens) of the KL gap.

source_check.correct: Both crosscoders reduce KL divergence by 59% over full responses and 78% over the early-response window. The early window comprises response tokens 2–10; token 1 was excluded.
source_check.locator_found: Section 3.2, footnote 9 and paragraph following Figure 4.
source_check.problem: The stated early-response window omits the exclusion of token 1.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 2B base and Gemma-2-2b-it
rows.operation_detail: Replaced the chat activation reconstruction with the crosscoder reconstruction error and compared its behavioral information with the chat reconstruction.
rows.measure: Relative KL reduction from error replacement versus chat reconstruction
rows.value: For full responses, the chat error term achieved slightly better KL reduction than the chat reconstruction for both crosscoders.
rows.uncertainty: 95% confidence intervals shown in Figure 4; exact intervals not stated in text
rows.note: The authors interpret this as evidence that the reconstruction error retains at least as much behavioral information as the learned dictionary for full responses.
rows.check: Bears on V5 completeness: over full responses the error term carries at least as much behavioural information as the dictionary.

rows.subject: Gemma 2 2B base and Gemma-2-2b-it
rows.operation_detail: Replaced the chat activation reconstruction with the crosscoder reconstruction error and compared its behavioral information with the chat reconstruction.
rows.measure: Relative KL reduction from error replacement versus chat reconstruction
rows.value: For the first 9 tokens, error replacement performed more than twice worse than the reconstruction for both crosscoders.
rows.uncertainty: 95% confidence intervals shown in Figure 4; exact intervals not stated in text
rows.note: The authors say the dictionaries capture early response-framing behavior better than longer-generation behavior.
rows.check: Bears on V5 completeness: over the first 9 tokens the dictionary captures more than twice what the error term does, but recovery is still incomplete.

source_check.correct: The early-response evaluation uses tokens 2–10, excluding token 1. For both crosscoders, error replacement leaves more than twice the KL divergence of reconstruction replacement; this does not establish that the dictionary recovers more than twice as much information.
source_check.locator_found: Section 3.2, footnote 9, Figure 4 and following paragraph.
source_check.problem: The token window is imprecise, and the verdict-fix gloss overinterprets the residual-KL comparison.

rows.subject: Gemma-2-2b-it
rows.operation_detail: Applied activation steering with individual BatchTopK chat decoder directions during generation.

conditions.value: α = 1 for latent 70149; α = 5 for latent 20384

rows.measure: Qualitative generated response under steering

rows.subject: Gemma 2 2B base and Gemma-2-2b-it
rows.operation_detail: Measured cosine similarity between decoder vectors for chat-only and base-only latent pairs.
rows.measure: Number of high-cosine chat-only/base-only latent pairs and activation divergence
rows.value: 109 pairs had cosine similarity greater than 0.9; 60% of pairs primarily activated on different contexts.
rows.note: The authors present this as evidence of latent decoupling and also note that similar decoder directions can be used in different contexts.
rows.check: Bears on V5 canonicity: under L1, 109 chat-only/base-only twin pairs (cosine > 0.9) split one concept across two latents, and 60% of pairs fire mostly on different contexts. 'Partial' here means that V5's canonical-units claim holds only incompletely.

statements.correction: Appendix I.2 compares DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B with Nemotron-Research-Reasoning-Qwen-1.5B after extended RL training. Table 1 reports 59 L1 fine-tuning-only latents, of which 58 (98.3%) are classified as false attributions by Latent Scaling. BatchTopK identifies zero fine-tuning-only latents at the stated norm threshold. These results bear on dictionary interpretation and method dependence during an explicit RL reasoning stage; they do not establish completeness or seed stability.
statements.problem: The blanket training-stage gap overlooks Appendix I.2, which explicitly examines additional RL training for reasoning and reports loss-dependent latent misattribution. Empirical completeness and seed stability remain untested there.

statements.correction: Gemma 2 2B base/chat all-latent replacement reduces KL divergence by 59% over full responses and 78% over response tokens 2–10, for both L1 and BatchTopK crosscoders; Section 3.2, footnote 9.
statements.problem: The percentages match the text, but the early-response window excludes the first response token.

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: L1 norm-based chat-only classification often misattributes features, while dictionary reconstruction leaves substantial behavioral information in the error term, especially over full responses (R1, R11, R14, R15).

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: L1 crosscoders in the reported Gemma, Llama, Qwen, and Meditron comparisons
reader_labels.reason: Many latents labeled model-specific by decoder norms are also reflected in base-model reconstruction or error, with false attribution rates reaching 98.3% in the reported table (R1, R3, R5, R7, R9, R11).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: BatchTopK crosscoders and tested behavioral evaluations
reader_labels.reason: BatchTopK substantially reduces reported artifacts and finds interpretable, causally relevant latents, but some false attributions remain in the table and reconstruction errors still contain behavioral information; the paper also cannot distinguish novel features from shifted existing features (R2, R4, R6, R10, R12, R14, R16).
